routes.description: Establish that neither determined nor undetermined action gives agents the ultimate authorship required for philosophical free will.
routes.successCriteria: Show that actions arise from force or unchosen wants whose causal histories never terminate in self-created control, while explaining practical agency without ultimate desert.

motionBridge.description: Connect the absence of control over determining causes and desires to the conclusion that voluntary action lacks ultimate authorship.

centralBridges.description: Establish that determined events inherit prior causes while undetermined events are uncontrolled, leaving neither branch as agent-authored control.
Establish that conduct follows either force or motivating wants and that agents do not independently choose the wants governing action.
Trace character and choice through upbringing, genetics, circumstances, and dispositions without reaching a self-created source.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how deterrence, prevention, rehabilitation, and compassion remain available without attributing ultimate moral desert.
Account for moral motivation and social restraint through causally formed desires rather than an independently chosen will.

routes.description: Establish that determined agents can possess meaningful freedom when conduct belongs to them, is voluntary, and lacks relevant coercive constraints.
routes.successCriteria: Show that freedom need not require ultimate self-creation, that voluntary agency admits context-sensitive degrees, and that causal description does not exhaust personal or ethical meaning.

motionBridge.description: Connect attributable, voluntary, and substantially unconstrained conduct to a defensible form of freedom despite causal determination.

centralBridges.description: Preserve a meaningful distinction between compelled conduct and action attributable to the person as its relevant source.
Explain freedom and its absence through degrees of voluntary control and context-sensitive impediments rather than causation alone.
Establish that interpersonal responsibility and first-person agency contain semantic and ethical dimensions not exhausted by third-person causal description.
Show how action may genuinely belong to a person while also arising through processes that the person did not deliberately manufacture.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Support the nonreductive account by treating conscious understanding as temporally and socially constituted rather than a static internal object.
Preserve the richer normative meaning of moral intuition against reduction to psychological or evolutionary causation.

sections.title: Determination, randomness, and ultimate control
sections.rationale: The motion turns first on whether either causal determination or its absence can provide the kind of authorship required for free action.

sections.title: Unchosen desires and voluntary action
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether acting from one's own motives is enough for freedom or merely transmits causal factors the agent never selected.

sections.title: Causal sourcehood and first-person agency
sections.rationale: The competing routes depend on whether causal histories exhaust agency or leave a first-person and personally attributable dimension of action intact.

sections.title: Responsibility, desert, and interpersonal ethics
sections.rationale: The consequences of each account depend on whether responsibility requires ultimate desert or can instead operate as a graded interpersonal and ethical practice.

sections.title: Causal explanation and moral meaning
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether a causal account of moral motivation replaces normative agency or can coexist with the richer meanings used in ethical life.
